grammar.gloss: The form on every verb card is a tense — the casual twin of ます.
An ichidan verb drops る and adds ない. する → しない, 来る → こない.
One rule for all eight endings — く→かない, む→まない. う→わない, and ある→ない.
ない is an i-adjective, so the plain past is the かった rule you already have.
The plain past is the te-form with て swapped for た, で for だ.
The plain copula. だった, じゃない, じゃなかった — and never after an i-adjective.
The casual yes and no. A plain question drops か and rises instead.
Have ever done it — an experience, not an event that happened.
Some of the things you do, not all of them and not in order. It ends in する.
Please don't — the ない form in the slot where ～てください takes the te-form.

grammar.pattern: だれに なにを あげます
grammar.gloss: You do the giving, and the gift moves away from you. Write it in kana, not 上げる.

grammar.pattern: だれから／だれに なにを もらいます
grammar.gloss: You do the receiving. The person it came from takes から or に.

grammar.pattern: だれが なにを くれます
grammar.gloss: Someone else gives, and it lands on you. The subject is no longer you.
The particles say who is on each side. が before the giver means it came to you.

grammar.pattern: 貸す／借りる／返す ≠ あげる／もらう
grammar.gloss: Lending is temporary and giving is not. 貸してください keeps it a loan.
Doing something for someone as a favour. The same caution as あげる applies.
Someone does it for you, unasked. This is the くれる inside every ください.

grammar.pattern: ～てくれますか／～てくれませんか
grammar.gloss: Asking for the favour. The negative question is the softer of the two.
You got someone to do it. Your sentence, their action — the giver takes に.
Because. Straight onto a verb or an い-adjective; a noun or な-adjective takes だ first.
The same reason, said more softly — and な where から took だ.
But. It attaches to a finished sentence, plain or polite, either way.
And then. The te-form joining two verbs in the order they happened.
While. Stop before ます, add ながら — two actions at once, one person doing both.
When. A whole clause standing in front of an ordinary noun meaning "moment".
The book I bought, the person who speaks. The same slot 時 used, with no 時 in it.

grammar.pattern: noun or な-adjective + になる
grammar.gloss: Become. The に is what a noun or a な-adjective needs before なる — 病気になる, 元気になる.
What's wrong? どう, the past of する, and か — a stock question with no new word in it.
Become, from an adjective. Drop the い and add く — 悪い to 悪くなる, with いい going irregular as よくなる.
Want to do it. Drop ます, add たい, and the whole thing behaves like an i-adjective.

grammar.pattern: たくない / たかった
grammar.gloss: Don't want to, and wanted to — the かった rule you already have from 高かった.
Want a thing, not an action. ほしくない, ほしかった — an i-adjective like any other.

grammar.pattern: 何が + たい / ほしい + か
grammar.gloss: Asking what someone wants — the only safe way to talk about another person's wants.
What you have decided to do. A plan, not a want.

grammar.pattern: つもりはない / つもりでした
grammar.gloss: No such plan, and a plan that was. つもり is a noun, so both come free.
Let's. You are proposing and expecting the other person to come along.
Would you like to? The same proposal with the answer left open.

grammar.pattern: ichidan: drop る, add られる
grammar.gloss: Able to do it. する has no rule and becomes できる; 来る becomes 来られる, read こられる.

grammar.pattern: godan: last sound to the え row, add る
grammar.gloss: One move for all nine endings — 書ける, 泳げる, 話せる, 待てる, 死ねる, 呼べる, 読める, 買える.
What you can do takes が, where the plain verb took を.
A skill with no verb in the sentence at all. できる sits straight on the noun.

grammar.pattern: dictionary form + ことができる
grammar.gloss: The same ability, with nothing conjugated. Any verb, no group to sort, and the object keeps を.

grammar.pattern: ます-stem + やすい / にくい
grammar.gloss: Easy to, hard to — a claim about the thing, not about you. Both inflect like い-adjectives.

grammar.pattern: plain clause + と言いました
grammar.gloss: と goes straight onto the plain form — no gap, no punctuation, nothing in between.
A noun or な-adjective clause keeps だ in front of と. です never appears there.
What someone has been saying, rather than one thing they said once.
What you heard, with no source named — 聞く slots into the same frame 言う did.
What you think, marked as your view rather than stated as fact.
The negative usually goes in the clause rather than on 思う. With は, 思いません is normal — そうは思いません.
A view you have held for a while, not one you are forming on the spot.

grammar.pattern: 〜と言っていました。〜と思います。
grammar.gloss: Their words, then yours — attributed separately so neither is mistaken for the other.
Shall we? ましょう with か on the end stops assuming the answer and asks for it instead.
The casual invitation. The ない form asked as a question, with no か and the voice going up.

grammar.pattern: topic + は + 都合がいい／都合が悪い
grammar.gloss: Whether a day suits you. One new noun on いい and 悪い, which you have had since the describing chapter.
If — the plain past plus ら, on verbs, adjectives and nouns alike.
Once that has happened — and unlike 時, the happening is what makes the rest possible.
Whenever this, automatically that. Never a request or a plan after it.
書けば, 読めば, 食べれば, すれば, 来れば. No exceptions — 買えば, あれば.

grammar.pattern: い → ければ / noun + なら
grammar.gloss: 高ければ, and いい's irregular よければ. Nouns take なら, never ば.
You'd better — past for the advice, plain ない for the warning against.

grammar.pattern: plain past + から／ので + 困っています
grammar.gloss: What went wrong, then the fact that you are stuck. The reason comes first, as it always does in Japanese.
It broke, and so it cannot be used. The te-form carrying cause rather than sequence.
Wanting somebody else to do it, where ～たい only ever wanted to do it yourself.
X is Y — the fundamental copula.
Confirmation / softening (\"It is, isn't it?\")
I came from ~ (origin pattern)

grammar.gloss: the thanks exchange

あまり and ぜんぜん require a negative verb ending (～ません)
Please do ~. Ichidan verbs drop る and add て.
A verb ending in く takes いて; ぐ takes いで.
The largest group — う, つ and る all become って.
む, ぬ and ぶ all become んで; す becomes して.
Doing it now, or doing it as a rule.
Did ~. Swap ます for ました; every verb behaves the same way.
Did not ~. ません picks up でした behind it.
Was ~. Nouns and na-adjectives swap です for でした.
Was ~. An i-adjective drops い and takes かった — never でした.
How was ~?
Makes a noun out of a verb — 食べる becomes 食べ物, the thing you eat.
Counter for cupfuls and bowlfuls. The sound changes at one, three and six.
Not very ~. The polite way to say something was bad.
The verb for wearing changes with where the thing goes — shoulders down, waist down, or on your head.
A colour is a noun and an adjective — 赤いかばん describes the bag, かばんは赤です names the colour.
